Mr. Speaker, for over a year and a half the people living in the Atlantis Housing Complex at 143 Ryland Avenue in Bible Hill, Nova Scotia, have been fighting to get door-to-door mail delivery to their homes. All the units have separate sidewalks and similar service comes all the way up to their units and then past them to the next houses.
Because of a very small technicality, these people, many of whom are seniors, have been denied door-to-door service. In the last several months I have been in touch with officials at Canada Post many times regarding this issue. Although they have been accessible and co-operative, my constituents still do not have a satisfactory resolution to their problem.
This case is now under its final appeal and I urge the post office officials to apply common sense and extend this service to 143 Ryland Avenue.

Mr. Speaker, over the last few weeks we have heard a lot of talk about democracy and the supremacy of the will of the people. The GST debate is a case in point. It is no secret that the people of Canada overwhelmingly reject the GST. Over 80 per cent of all Canadians oppose this regressive tax, and the number continues to grow. In fact, from my riding of Nipissing alone, I have received well over 6,000 protest cards on the GST and how it will escalate the cost of such basic services as hydroelectricity.
Despite this opposition, the government is continuing to push ahead, regardless of what the people believe. Who is being undemocratic here when the will of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance can prevail over the will of millions of Canadians? How democratic is it when people with incomes of $100,000 or more pay
October 9, 1990

$1,600 less in income tax today? How democratic is it when corporations get their taxes cut, only to have them shifted to a segment of the population that is being hit with 32 separate tax increases?

Mr. Speaker, as November 1 approaches, Canadians who make their living from the sea, fishers, shore workers and their families across the country are facing a devastating winter. The cause of this crisis is our own government with its blind determination to gut the
unemployment insurance system while sacrificing the needs of Canadian workers.
Last November, the New Democratic House leader asked the Minister of Employment to introduce legislation for the variable entrance requirements. In a callous disregard for the plight of seasonal workers and workers in areas of high unemployment, she refused.
Had the minister followed my colleague's advice, representatives of fishers and shore workers from the west and east coast would not be here today scrambling to avert a disaster.
The New Democratic Party has opposed Bill C-21 because of the harm it will cause. The minister is well aware that had she brought forward legislation last fall for the variable entrance requirement, we would not be in the mess we find ourselves in today.
I call on the Minister of Employment to give up her childish policy of her way or no way, because we know in this instance her way is wrong. Avert a disaster. Withdraw Bill C-21. Bring in the variable entrance requirements now.

Mr. Speaker, the government has consistently given support to grain farmers under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the Advance Payments for Crops Act.
A further step to aid farmers with their cash flow problems would be to reintroduce interest free cash advances. I am encouraged to hear that a working meeting of farmers, industry and government representatives was held in Winnipeg on October 5 to consider this matter. That this meeting did take place is reassuring news to all Canadian farmers.
I urge the group to present their recommendations as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the bloody events in Old Jerusalem this past weekend have prompted a stronger call by the international community for a just solution of the Palestinian situation.

October 9, 1990
This type of violent activity can no longer be tolerated and should be dealt with immediately by the Security Council, with the full support of the Government of Canada.
As we approach the annual United Nations debate on Palestinians, I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to urge all members of the Security Council to accept, if offered, a resolution calling for an international presence, either in the form of UN observers or officials from the office of the Secretary General.
It is only in this way that attempts to tie the invasion of Kuwait to a settlement of the Palestinian question can be pre-empted. The international community can then work further in solidarity against force and aggression toward a peaceful and permanent solution of the Palesti-nian-Israeli situation.
Listening to both Palestinians and Israelis this summer, I know, Mr. Speaker, that both sides want peace. The international community should help set up the process to achieve a lasting peace.

Mr. Speaker, Public Works is planning the construction of a parking lot and a shopping mall under the Parliament of Canada, at the cost of $68 millions. Many people are opposed to that because of the environment, on the grounds that the historical character of the buildings must be preserved, and so on.
Mr. Speaker, with that money, we could build 136 shelters for incapacitated senior citizens, 250 youth centers as well as housing for the poor across Canada.
I am against that project. I already have an outdoor parking spot on the Hill, like all factory workers in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this morning the Prime Minister announced to the Commonwealth ministers responsible for women's
affairs how much the Canadian government is doing for women. What a surprise this is for the women of Canada! Particularly offensive is his assertion that his government is dealing with violence against women, which is a serious problem in every country of the world, and Canada is no exception.
Today, women gathered on Parliament Hill to display 150 banners dealing with the reality of women's lives. Nearly a majority of them were about violence against women. In Canada, one out of every two women seeking refuge at a shelter for battered women is turned away because of lack of space. Thirty-seven per cent of the murders in Canada are related to family violence. Almost 100 women a year die at the hands of men they live with or have lived with. This government's policies- cuts to women's programming and capping of funds for battered women's shelters-are costing women their lives. This, Mr. Speaker, is the reality for Canadian women.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, few would argue that skills training will play a vital role in Canada's future economic growth and competitiveness. Yet, too often, we overlook the fundamentals. Basic fundamentals-basic literacy and numeracy skills-are the foundation for skills development. We must then begin with the basics, basic skills and their formation.
Canadians recognize that the seeds for skills development occur during childhood. Such an observation adds to the appreciation of our children as our most vital resource. Our children must receive greater attention.
The successful completion of the world summit for children is a good starting point, helping to focus attention on the urgent needs and problems of our children.
With the creation of the children's bureau and the pledge that the welfare of our children will be a high priority, I, like the families and children across Canada, look forward to the initiatives which will arise from this agenda.
If we are going to progress and have the basic skills to compete, our children must be a higher priority. In this light, I readily applaud our government's commitment to do so.

Mr. Speaker, the lessening of tension in Europe has led to a decision to bring 1,400 NATO troops back to Canada. More recently, there has been a Soviet-American agreement to reduce troops and military hardware in Europe. This will facilitate a further Canadian withdrawal of its NATO forces, which number 6,200 army and air force personnel.
It is time for the Department of National Defence to do some serious re-examination of its policy on base closures. For example, where will the 2,000 air force personnel be stationed when they come back?
The Department of National Defence now has an opportunity to correct or at least partially correct the error made in closing CFB Summerside and leaving Prince Edward Island as the only province without a military base. Leaving 413 Squadron, Search and Rescue, in Summerside will complement the helicopter repair business being recruited to locate on the base, will encourage the location of similar types of industries in Summerside, maintain Search and Rescue in its proven best location and show that DND has the ability to adapt to changing world realities and implement policies which make military and economic sense.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress again the enormous importance of housing in this country, both as a material and social asset.
Canadians in general are well housed, but our houses are getting old. More than 20 percent of all houses in Canada are now over 40 years old, and this will increase to 50 percent by the end of the century. Many of these houses, which are an important source of affordable housing, will need major repairs. In fact, some 10 percent of our apartments are already in need of serious attention.
The month of October was designated National Renovation Month in Canada. The federal government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Canada, will
work together with the renovation industry to protect and promote this important national investment.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Canadian Home Builders' Association and the Bank of Montreal for their role in raising awareness on this important issue.

Mr. Speaker, in June in this House I raised the question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare's $4 million cut to the budget of the National Health Research and Development Program.
Over the summer I was in touch with leading researchers and learned firsthand of the damage caused by these cuts. It is important to understand that this is the government's only program for funding applied health research, which includes preventive health care, health promotion, disease prevention, work place hazards, cancer prevention and native health care.
As incredible as it may seem, all innovative health care research has been put on hold or permanently cancelled by this short-sighted government. One University of Quebec researcher affected by the cuts proposed to study the risks of cancer due to asbestos exposure in the general environment. The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows as well as anyone that it is far less expensive to prevent cancer than to treat it.
I urge the minister to restore the funding for health care research now.

Chalk one up for Mother Nature, Mr. Speaker. This fall the Adams River in British Columbia has witnessed the largest migratory run of sockeye salmon in 77 years. speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her question because it is an issue of grave concern to all Canadians, not just to Canadian women.
The government's program with respect to family violence spans a number of different departments. It is a $40 million initiative. I am pleased to respond with respect to what the Department of Justice is doing.

October 9, 1990
Oral Questions
The Department of Justice has made the protection of women from violence a major focus of its work. This includes reform of the Criminal Code. The law governing sexual violence was amended in 1983, and the department is assessing the impact of those changes.
In addition, we are analysing measures to deal specifically with violent pornography. We have funded research to other projects; for example, a television program to inform the general public about the existing law of sexual assault and an evaluation of programs for men who batter their spouses or lovers.
Also, in the area of policy development, the department has set up a departmental committee to develop policies relating to women, especially violence against women, and it participates in an interdepartmental committee developing policy on family violence.
With respect to the administration of justice, the department has provided support for conferences and seminars designed to sensitize justice professionals on sex equality issues, especially as they relate to violence against women.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for her very comprehensive report on what her department is doing.
I think that action has to speak louder than words. I believe it is time that the Minister of Justice brought the attorneys general of the provinces together to amend the Criminal Code to protect women.

Mr. Speaker, when one o'clock was called, I had just finished reading from an international report which basically said that the reason Canada is not pursuing sustainable development is simply that this government lacks the requisite national will.
The question is: How can this government be so short-sighted? Does this government not realize that sustainable development applies to every field of economic activity?
In the case of agriculture, the Canadian farmer is struggling. Five major droughts in the prairies in the 1980s have certainly brought home the effects of climate change. The contamination of groundwater, the result of fertilizers and pesticides, is but the tip of the iceberg as are indeed the concerns about food safety. It is clear that
Supply
this nation needs new arrangements to secure a food system that is both economically and environmentally viable.
Thrning to forestry, properly managed forests will bring together two seemingly irreconcilable objectives, economic and environmental. On the one hand is the preservation of the basic resource for our largest export industry. On the other are the benefits of biological diversity and wildlife habitat. An improperly managed forest simply means that we in this nation will face a race to see who will suffer most: the next generation's jobs or the next generation's ecosystem.
The point is that you simply cannot have a strong economy if you do not make protection of the environment your number one priority. If there is any doubt about this, then I would simply ask the members present to look around and take a look at what we and our international partners and competitors have done with the fishing industry.
The issue is: wherein lies the problem? The problem lies with this government. This government believes that sustainable development is simply a cost as opposed to the prevention of a cost before it occurs. This government indeed looks upon sustainable development only as a cost and fails to understand the tremendous opportunities that are involved.
I would suggest to members on the other side of the House that they take a look at West Germany and ask themselves why it is that West Germany is both the environmental leader of Europe as well as the economic leader of Europe. It is no coincidence. One follows the other.
When will this government begin to understand the demands, the needs, and the opportunities of the 1990s? There are many solutions to the degradation of the environment, all of which have positive implications for the economy.
Is it a coincidence that Japan has cut its consumption per unit produced of fuel by 30 per cent? Is it a coincidence that Japan has cut its material usage by over 43 per cent? Japan does not necessarily have the best reputation, as I discussed earlier this morning, in the world in terms of environmental matters; but in terms of the development of its own economy the Japanese have understood the application of sustainable development to industrial development. It is in the process of winning

Supply
the battle, while we under this sterile government are losing the battle.
Turning to new technologies, 20 per cent of the world is in the process of polluting it for the other 80 per cent. Over the course of the next 30 years as the Third World or the developing world begins to improve its standard of living, it too, if it follows our lead, will begin to pollute. As the population of the world doubles from five billion to ten billion, the problems without the development of new technologies will simply become unbearable.
This is an enormous opportunity for a country like Canada to take the lead, to build a whole new industrial base, not on the provision of arms as others have done but on the creation of new technologies to win the ultimate battle, that is the battle for the preservation of this earth.

The environment does not bear only a social cost. It also provides a magnificent opportunity to lay a new industrial base, as the United States did in 1910 with the automotive industry and both the States and Japan did between 1945 and 1950 with computer technology. We could take the lead in industrial development. The time is right. Now we need to be imaginative. We need initiative.

In conclusion, I began by talking about the economy. I began talking about some of our problems. I now end having talked about sustainable development and the tremendous opportunities that it provides. Let us never forget that the protection of the environment is a moral value. It needs no economic support. Preservation of this planet is the essence of what humanity must fight for over the next 25 years. Let us also realize that sustainable development provides us with the opportunity in regard to our economic dilemma. It gives this country the chance to lay a whole new industrial base and pick up where we have often lost. It gives this country the opportunity to show the moral leadership that the world so requires. It gives this country the opportunity to show the kind of moral leadership that national unity requires if, indeed, Canadians are going to believe in something beyond themselves.
The issue is, are we as a nation up to the challenge? I believe we are. We believe in this planet. The time has now come to take the lead in preserving it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to be able to take part in this debate today because I think that when we look at it, 1990 will go down in history as a major turning point in world history.
The scope and range of the developments of the past 12 months really rival anything we have seen since the Second World War. We are on the verge of a new era that may seem threatening to some people, but I like to look on it as offering magnificent opportunities for countries and firms prepared to master the challenges we now face.
We in this government intend to meet those challenges not by being negative, but by building a strong co-operative partnership between government, the private sector, and provincial governments to exploit the competitive opportunities of globalization.
Let me review how quickly things have changed in the past year. I guess the most significant one is the total collapse of the U.S.S.R. They have a bankrupt ideology, ethnic tensions. The ideology of state ownership was obviously not working so something had to be done. Now we see the logic of the market principles.
This magnitude of change has been underlined with the destruction of the Berlin wall and the very real rush for eastern European countries to move in and try to set up democratic governments similar to ones we see in the western world. The unification of Germany took place just a few days ago. In the other end of the world we see

Supply
the reversal of 40 years of apartheid in South Africa. We admire the courage of the people in Latin America who are now throwing off the wasted governments of dictatorship and corruption and are pushing for democracy and freer markets. Of course, we see Mexico moving in this direction to a freer market economy.
Across the Pacific we see Japan and the four tigers, and now the emerging cubs of Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia continue to outpace growth everywhere in the world. Inter-regional investments are leaping the national frontiers and moving into these other countries.
Finally, the economies of Europe have discovered with renewed fervour the promise of co-operation and open borders. The second half of the 1980s marked a renaissance in the European ideal leading to the stirring prospect of a strong and united European market for close to half a billion people in the next few years-half a billion people, a strong market. A free market-a free movement in those areas.
It is exciting both politically and economically. It is an exciting time for everyone interested in building on Canadian strengths through new or expanded trade investment and technology ties.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a time for wringing hands and deploring the lost opportunities of the 1960s, 1970s and the 1980s, but a time to build on the promise and success of what we initiated in the 1980s.
We are a government that is acutely aware that we must look outward and forward, rather than inward and backward. Our policies must respond to these challenges and seize the opportunities because failure to grasp these emerging opportunities for Canada in the global economy in this decade of the 1990s would doom Canada to second class citizenship status. This government will not make that mistake.
We know these global forces and developments mean that Canada will face increased competitiveness as well as tremendous opportunities in years to come. This government will elaborate an ever more sophisticated and complex approach to our trade and industrial policies and to our trade relations. We will build on the achievement of the past six years. We will adapt our
policies to meet the constant challenges posed by rapid global developments.
We know the challenges we have to be aware of-continued globalization of industries through the investment decisions of multinational enterprises. These multinational enterprises now produce and sell their products wherever they can reap the greatest advantage.
We accept the increasing importance of the investment and service sectors complementing the more traditional resources and manufacturing sectors. We are aware of the increasing risk, largely due to the United States Congressional protectionism and heavy handedness, of a shift to unilateralism, with key decisions of trading issues being reached by a bilateral basis along the Washington-Tokyo and the Washington-Brussels axis, with the interests of smaller players like Canada, sometimes ignored and forgotten.
We recognize that the Gulf crisis has hastened development of a potential third global energy crunch which, if not well managed, will undercut new opportunities. We realize that the greater integration of eastern Europe into the global economy will place great strains on available capital-capital, of course, is the engine of growth-and increase political pressure for more debt relief.
We know that debt relief also represents an awesome challenge for both developing and developed countries. The total debt load of developing countries now surpasses $1.3 trillion, with little immediate prospect that the trend can be reversed.
Many LDCs remain mired in slow growth, poor trade prospects and continued corruption. We know that. We recognize the challenge that this presents for this government.
On a brighter note, however, Mr. Speaker, we are pleased by the new market orientation of many Latin American economies. It is an encouraging sign that there remains potential for growth in the development world.
Finally, we are alert to the emergencies of the environment as an economic and trade related issue because our fragile environment calls for responsible trade and industrial policies. At the same time, we will need to be wary of green protectionism, the abuse of environmental principles with restrictions that meet narrow protectionist ends rather than environmental protection which we
October 9, 1990

see starting to emerge and restrictions aimed at responsible forestry practices where Canada can be particularly vulnerable. We have to be careful of those things.
The rapid pace of change that we have seen makes everyone a little uneasy. It makes Canadian citizens a little uneasy. They are fraught with risk, we know that. I prefer to see it as filled with promise. The challenge is to respond constructively and thus exploit the opportunities for growth.
It is too easy for the critic opposite to throw up assertions that we need his constructive analysis of these changes and a co-operative approach to mastering them. That is what we need, we need co-operation.
The conclusions we draw and the policies we erect are critical to Canada's ability to grow in this new interdependent, highly competitive world. The world is shrinking. The last time that the world faced such momentous change was more than four decades ago. The result was a bold new global system to create order out of the chaos of 15 years of depression and the Second World War.
Based upon an unselfish United States commitment to liberalism and multilateralism, institutions like the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the General Agreement on Thriffs and Trade, known as the GATT, and the United Nations brought about the greatest increase in economic and political well-being in the history of the world. If we can keep the risk in check, 1990 offers potential to unleash another round of similarly creative forces, forces that achieved so much in the 25 years after 1945.
Canadians will have to accept the globalization of the economy and the pressures of market realities cannot be ignored. At best their impact can be delayed for only a short period.
No government can long develop its trade policy or its domestic economic agenda in isolation from the realities of the global marketplace. This is what previous Liberal governments did in the sixties and the seventies. They followed a policy that sought to isolate Canadians from the international economy. The result of course was the decline in our competitiveness.
This government is determined not to repeat the mistakes of our predecessors. For a middle power like Canada, our commitment to the principles of reciprocity, non-discrimination, and transparency cannot be over
Supply
emphasized. It means that a stable, open, non-discriminatory, global economic system must remain our number one goal as we adapt to a rapidly globalizing economy. It means that we must recognize that liberalized trade is a two-way street. Canadians not only benefit from open, secure access to foreign markets, but Canadians also benefit from foreign competition in their own market.
The challenge of competitiveness is the best medicine for any business. One only has to ask Northern Telecom, Alcan, Spar Aerospace, Lavalin, or any of the hundreds of successful Canadian companies which have found that meeting the competition at home means beating the competition abroad.
The government is acutely aware of the importance of creating a spirit of entrepreneurship. We understand the critical role of international trade to Canadians. Indeed, October is export month and our ad campaign is aimed at making Canadians more aware of the importance of our international trade effort to their jobs, to their incomes, and to their economic well-being. The ads are in a language even the opposition should understand. We are responding to the competitive challenge at home and abroad with the following priorities. I will outline them briefly.
We will pursue and enhance access to our major market, the United States, which we gained through the free trade agreement and through the General Agreement on Thrifts and Trade.
We will continue to push strongly and constructively for a substantive and large conclusion to the multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva.
We will continue to explore with our European trading partners how we will jointly build the right kind of instruments to ensure that Canadian entrepreneurs will be able to reap the benefits of the European Renaissance symbolized by 1992.
We are prepared to build on our initiatives towards Latin America, going beyond our OAS membership and a free trade agreement with Mexico, and build new partnerships throughout Latin America.
Finally, we will continue to pursue policies and partnerships that will ensure that Canada will be a major player in the Asia/Pacific region.

Supply
We are working on these priorities with much intensity through the Departments of External Affairs and International Trade.
There are challenges that exist when these things happen and we know what the challenges are. The challenge of the 1990s is to get our house in order. Today's debate places the spotlight on this critical issue. I thank the opposition for creating this opportunity. I deplore, however, their negativism. We, in Canada, must speak with one voice, a voice that tells the world that Canadians are confident about their future. We cannot continually allow the negative comments that come forward strictly for the political agenda to mar the opportunities that face us in the future.
More than ever, we must attain the national agenda that we have before us. It is critical to the achievement of our international goals.
Since 1984, the government has sought sustained, non-inflationary economic growth. We have pursued a productive employment strategy, creating more than one million jobs. In the past year alone, our policies have resulted in a net increase of over 150,000 jobs.
I know you are signalling me about my time, Mr. Speaker. I would like to cariy on because there is much more to say. I would like to address for a moment the Economic Council of Canada.
In the Economic Council of Canada report, one always hears very isolated facts. I have heard it from the opposition. The Economic Council of Canada states clearly that controlling inflation "is a policy objective that benefits Canadians in all walks of life-In a sense, inflation control is a public good, and this means that all Canadians should contribute to the avoidance of unnecessary pressures on prices and costs."
That observation succinctly summarizes a critical element of the policy thrust of the government. The fact is, through 1989 and into this year, underlying inflationary pressures were significant. These pressures were taking their deadly aim on costs, on workers whose jobs would be lost when their products were priced out of markets, and on all Canadians who depend on fixed incomes.
For example, during the second quarter, total unit labour costs-a critical measure of a country's competitiveness-were growing at an annual rate of 6.6 per cent
per annum. That is not only a rate higher than in 1989, but half again higher than in the U.S.
As well, through the first quarter, borrowing both by consumers and business-another measure of inflationary pressure-continued to advance at a rate reflecting an overheated economy. In April, consumer credit was up 12.4 per cent over the same period in 1989, more than double the American rate. Mortgage credit was up 17.1 per cent, a growth about two and a half times faster than nominal income growth in Canada.
The government has acted on its obligation to use the levers available to ensure that these dangerous and destructive forces were not allowed to proceed unchecked. In such an environment, as Minister Wilson has said: "Interest rates had to rise. With the strong inflationary pressures and demand for credit already present in the economy, it would have been irresponsible to reduce the cost of credit." This would only have encouraged further inflationary demands that would have been financed by a greater accumulation of corporate and personal debt. The inevitable result would have been explosive rounds of wage and price increases leading to an even more pronounced and longer-lasting slowdown that we currently face. We saw that in the early 1980s when inflation rose to double-digit rates. Then we had double-digit unemployment and interest rates rose to 22 per cent or 23 per cent.
This is not a might-happen scenario I have outlined, it is what did happen in the late 1970s, as inflation and interest rates soared. The consequence, as we all should remember, was the 1981-82 period with double-digit unemployment.
This is not the prospect Canadians face today, fortunately. Yes, we are going through a period that does involve pain and hardship. The government's policies, which we have been pursuing since the start of our mandate six years ago, have positioned us so that Canadians will not suffer the truly drastic and destructive economic conditions of the start of this decade. We are now in a position to weather the current storm and emerge stronger and more prosperous. This is surely what all Canadians, including my hon. friends in opposition, desire.
There are a number of other areas in which the council report and the direction of government policy are consistent. The council, for example, supports the direction of the government's unemployment insurance reforms,

away from income support and toward job retraining. Similarly, the council supports the kind of decentralized approach to regional development that the government has adopted through bodies such as ACOA.
I want to thank you very much for allowing me to participate. I would be happy to answer any questions which might come from the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member's intervention and what he said about sustainable development.
I wonder whether the hon. member would like to comment about sustainable development as practised by his government in the field of energy and natural resources? Would he comment about the fact that Canada has so far failed to ratify the Law of the Sea at the United Nations? That is a very important piece of legislation that would protect resources in the oceans.
Would he comment about the fact that over the last four years the Government of Canada has virtually eliminated energy research in the field of renewable sources of energy? Would he comment about the fact that over the last four years the Government of Canada has increased its dependence on fossil fuels, thus exacerbating for a long time to come the problem of climate warming because, as we all know, the consumption of fossil fuels leads to the production of greenhouse gases?
Would the hon. member comment about whether he is aware of the fact that the government is not spending one penny in the promotion of energy efficiency, which also makes good economic sense? Nevertheless, it is not being promoted in the budget of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Therefore, on that front, we have nothing positive to say, as he urged in his speech, to show a united front to the world? How can we if we have nothing to report that is positive in relation to the reduction of our dependence on fossil fuels, in promoting energy efficiency, and finally, in promoting alternative sources of energy? Canada has a tremendous endowment for a renewable source of energy, particularly in biomass. For that also we have no message to give to the rest of the world because the budgetary restrictions and cuts have eliminated these types of initiatives on the

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the things that we faced when we took office in 1984 was program spending that was increasing at approximately 14 per cent year after year after year.
I would like to bring to the attention of my hon. friend that the hon. Minister for International Trade, who was at that time Minister of Finance in the short lived government, brought in a budget, a budget in which he identified very clearly the problems that we would be going to be facing if we did not come to grips with the debt and a deficit that presently existed. He then put forward in his budget that he was going to increase the price of gasoline by 18 cents a gallon across the country.
We all know the result of that budget. We all know that it was defeated in this House of Commons irresponsibly by the Liberals and the NDP. In 1980 they went across the country and decried the budget of the hon. Minister for International Trade that was going to attack the deficit and the debt directly.
What I am suggesting to my hon. friend is that because of the economic situation that this country faced in 1984 when we as a government got a look at the books and saw the drastic position we were in, it was impossible for us to continue on with the programs. We had to cut program spending, which we were able to do, and we brought program spending down to 3.5 per cent. It was an unprecedented turnaround in the economy of this country, one that we had to do. You cannot do the kinds of things that that member over there is crying out to do when you have not got the money to pay the debts and pay for the programs of this country.
In 1984, we were actually borrowing $16 billion to live. We were not borrowing it just to pay the interest on the accumulated debt. We were borrowing $16 billion to pay old age security, to pay our health care programs. We were borrowing from foreign nations to live in this country because of the wild, irresponsible spending of the Liberal government between 1980 and 1984, and even previous to that.
Mr. Speaker, that member stands up and says we are not spending enough money on all of these programs. We are not deserting those areas. We are still doing the

Supply
research, but we are doing it in a more reasonable way and one that we can afford. We cannot afford the unreasonable, irresponsible kind of spending that went on with the Liberal government that brought us into this mess that we are in today.

Mr. Speaker, as you will recall, this morning I had indicated to you that I had spent much of the last five days travelling throughout my constituency, talking to farmers about the plight on the western prairies.
Firsthand I saw the piles of grain being dumped in yards throughout the entire western prairie countryside that I was visiting. In my constituency alone, I am sure there is not a single farmyard that does not have a pile of grain sitting in it because the system is not moving. The grain system is not moving the grain from the elevators to the ports for whatever export markets there might be.
That aside, Mr. Speaker, a lot of the farm people that I have been talking to have been telling me that in addition to higher grain prices, they need the interest-free cash advance. If their grain is not moving because the system cannot move it, the only way they can gain assistance is through loans from the banks. In fact, all of the national farm groups have called for the reinstatement of the interest-free cash advance.
My colleague from Athabasca drives through a lot of farm country to get to his home every weekend when he goes to visit his constituents. He must realize the difficulty that the farm population has throughout western Canada.
He talked at some length in his speech about government policy and the net increase in jobs that government policy has created. I tend to look at the net decrease in farm jobs that government policy has created.
I am convinced that government policy, removing the interest-free cash advance, is going to further increase the number of job losses on the farm and off the farm in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba.
Earlier today during Statements by Members, the colleague of the hon. member for Athabasca, the hon. member for Wild Rose, called for the reinstatement of the interest-free cash advance. I am wondering what the position of the member for Athabasca is on the interestfree cash advance. Does he support reinstatement of the same?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what a short memory we
have.
This government, with the leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister, for the first time in the history of this country was able to bring the number one agenda item to the GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Hade. It is being discussed now.
For the first time we are seeing the disruption in the farm community being addressed by working on and reducing the subsidies that the European Common Market and the United States have for the agriculture industry.
Having said that, my hon. friend mentioned that we could not move grain across the country. Certainly, we can move grain across the country, but there are no markets. The markets are dwindling because of the grain trade war that exists between the United States and the European Common Market. We all know that.
The hon. member asked me about support for the farmers in the agricultural community. Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you that no government in the history of this country since Confederation has been more generous and more supportive to the farming industry in Canada than this one.
Billions of dollars have gone into the agriculture industry, literally billions. The member also stands in this House and condemns the goods and services tax. Does he not recognize that the goods and services tax will put over $.25 billion into the farmers' pockets by the removal of the manufacturers' sales tax.
That member goes around, talks out of one side of his mouth and then the other. The prairie advances and those kinds of things, just watch us. Just watch and see what happens. This government has never deserted the farmer.

Mr. Speaker, I should say at the outset that I want to divide my time today in this most important debate between myself and the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell because we both have a specific area that we want to touch on.
I rise to speak briefly on the motion presented by my colleague:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to provide
Canadians with policies designed to assure full employment through
international competitiveness and consistent with the principles of
sustainable development.
Indeed, it is a most opportune time to take stock of just where this government is and where it is leading us through the current round of GATT negotiations.
The government seems bent and bound to avoid a debate in this House on these issues, and in fact has been quietly dismantling the support mechanisms of our marketing organizations while negotiating away the legislative base of our dairy organization and poultry marketing agencies that have brought stability to both the dairy and poultry sectors.
This government has been negotiating away the powers that were given by legislation passed in this House by elected members of Parliament. It has conducted secret negotiations behind closed doors in the GATT and in the free trade agreement. The government is undermining the programs that have served this nation well, and which are indeed the envy of the world.
In fact, when the Canadian documents were tabled in Geneva just over a week ago, we knew that they would provide both the measures of support and tariff equivalent calculations. These are suggestions put forward by the U.S.-the aggregate measures of support or the differences between the domestic price and what the world price is-and are identifying the difference as subsidies. The tariff equivalents are a series of tariff reductions that will be phased out over a period of 10 years, whether from 30 per cent down, 3 per cent per year, or from 40 per cent down, 4 per cent per year.
The dairy industry and poultry sectors of Canada should be exempt from these calculations or measures because they clearly do not make any sense for industries
Supply
that operate a planned production system in compliance with Article 11 of the GATT. But the exemption from the GATT was not addressed in the Canadian document. Rather, the Canadian position was that Canada should receive a credit to reduce the aggregate measure of support, but this is not acceptable.
The dairy industry has rejected the calculations of the market price support. The basis for 86 per cent of the aggregate measure of support calculation is simply the difference between Canadian milk prices and world prices. In this situation, world prices are simply U.S. prices, in close proximity to the Canada-U.S. borders. These prices for the aggregate measures of support of $2.2 billion are clearly misleading, and the government should admit this error and apologize to the dairy farmers of Canada.
The only direct subsidy for the dairy industry is $266 million for industrial milk and is designed to keep the consumer price of cheese, yogurt and butter at a low level. This subsidy only represents 12 per cent of the price received by producers for industrial milk and, of course, we have no subsidy on fluid milk. The aggregate measures of support are based on the false premise that production costs are equal in both Canada and the United States.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the dairy farmers of Canada have shown, beyond a doubt, that Canadian input costs are much higher and it is beyond the power of the Canadian dairy farmer to correct these differences. In fact, just this weekend, I gathered prices from a friend and a constituent of six major input costs on a dairy farm. They are shocking. These are differences between the cost of an operation in Middlesex county in Ontario and an operation in St. Clair county in the state of Michigan. Let me just cite those six examples.
First, let me give an example of the interest rates. The difference between the amount of interest, paid over a 10-year period on a $100,000 mortgage, between Ontario and the United States is $14,690, in favour of the American farmer. That is a difference of 22.4 per cent more interest that the Canadian farmer has to pay compared to his American counterpart.
Gasoline costs $1.35 per U.S. gallon and there is a tax rebate sent to the farmer on an annual basis, provided he buys gasoline with a 10 per cent ethanol content to make

Supply
sure that he shows concern for the environment because ethanol-based fuels are less polluting. Gasoline, delivered to a farm, in bulk, as of Thursday, was 54.9 cents a litre. The difference between that price and the U.S. price, converted to U.S. gallons, is 61.6 per cent higher in Ontario. When it comes to fertilizers, there is a difference of 20 per cent per tonne in favour of the American farmer, again.
When it comes to daiiy feed, there is a shocking example of a dairy supplement with 40 per cent protein. Again, these are two comparisons, made not more than 70 miles apart, one in Michigan and one in Ontario, and the Canadian price is 73 per cent higher in Ontario than it is in the United States. Machinery parts is another example. A package of six Case International French bottom plough points costs $115 Canadian in Emmett, Michigan. Those six points, made by the same company in Exeter Ontario, are $143.70, a difference of 24 per cent.
When we speak of veterinary supplies, the cost is 200 per cent higher in Canada. I am speaking here specifically of penicillin and streptomycin. In the United States, a 250 cc bottle sells for $19.55 Canadian, while a 100 cc bottle in Ontario costs $24, a cost difference of over 200 per cent.
While our government is working toward increasing the import levels allowed into Canada under the GATT, it is interesting to note that on November 1, 1990, 11 of the major milk producing states in the U.S. will be starting a system of production management or, as they call it, inventory control. Michigan, Wisconsin, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, Minnesota, Iowa, California, Texas, Washington, and Indiana are the states involved. This amounts to about 80 per cent of the milk produced in the United States with 1989 as the base year.
Just as the Canadian government is committing a sin by even talking about dismantling supply management systems, other countries like the United States and Europe are starting to see the necessity for the survival of their food growers. It will soon be impossible for Canadians even to have a TV commercial urging us to buy Canadian to keep our workers working, our producers producing.
Surely those who remember food conditions during the Second World War shudder at the Middle East situation that exists today and realize the absolute necessity for food grown at home.
I ask government members to realize that if they are going to open up up import quotas to give away yet more of our Canadian markets, they have a responsibility to ensure that our farmers are not being ripped off through higher input costs which place them in a non-competitive cost position. I also wish to ask them why they have failed not only to protect our producers but to ensure these GATT negotiations guarantee that any agricultural products entering this nation are produced in countries practising sustainable development.
We have the best marketing system in the world. This misguided government is responding to a few multinational traders in a way that is not acceptable to our own people.
The dairy farmers of Canada cannot accept the government's current position simply to claim a credit in the calculation of aggregate measure of support for supply management programs. Such a position is contradictory to the stated objective of the federal government to maintain a viable supply management program in Canada. Any commitment to place a ceiling on or to reduce the price of milk in Canada would automatically undermine one fundamental principle of supply management or planned production, which is to ensure fair and equitable returns to the producers.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure this afternoon to take part in the debate in support of my colleague's motion of non-confidence which states:
That this House condemn the Government for its failure to provide Canadians with policies designed to assure full employment through international competitiveness and consistent with the principles of sustainable development.
Mr. Speaker, as far as the government's economic policy is concerned, the Economic Council released on October 3, as you know, a report in which it condemns this government's policy. Allow me to quote from the report:
"-there is something inherently wrong in the way we tried to solve our economic problems in the past.

Further in the release is the following statement:
The annual review also indicates that new economic problems could arise if the decision-makers count only on high interest rates to fight inflation or if the various governments adopt divergent economic policies.
And further still, it reads:
"Canada's options are few and unappealing", according to the Council.
This government's economic policy is clearly wrong, Mr. Speaker. On the one hand, we have industries closing their doors because the free-trade agreement this government signed had devastating effects in the riding I have the honour to represent.
At the present time, the government is negotiating a new GAIT agreement. Of course, everyone agrees we should be part of GATT and have agreements with this international organization. However, there are some grave concerns with respect to the government's policies in this respect.
Mr. Speaker, the government opposite seems to prefer giving away the store first and negotiating afterwards. I would like to read to you part of a letter I received on September 4, 1990, from the Dairy Farmers of Canada, about the GATT negotiations. It reads as follows:
Deeply concerned, the Dairy Farmers of Canada would like to bring to your attention the enclosed policy statement about the use of aggregate measures of support in GATT negotiations.
Further on:
Applying a ceiling or reducing domestic support by way of an aggregate measure of support might eliminate altogether any resulting benefits. The Dairy Farmers of Canada are vigorously opposed to applying, in GATT negotiations any AMS commitment to programs subject to the provisions of Article XI.
Mr. Speaker, Article XI is the GATT article that allows supply management in Canada.
Despite these concerns and objections, we just heard our colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, himself a former minister of Agriculture, inform the House that the government has in fact submitted a position that includes the aggregate measure of support, and has done so against the will of the Dairy Farmers of Canada.

The Dairy Farmers of Canada are not the only organization to be concerned about the government's policy on external trade. I have another letter, this one dated September 18, 1990, signed by Mr. Jacques Proulx, president of the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, the UPA.
Mr. Proulx says in his letter, and I will read you parts of it:

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all this was dated September 18-if the hon. member would bother to listen, he would know-and this was the letter we received, as I said earlier, on that date.
What happened since then? Well, I just told you, Mr. Speaker. First of all, the worst scenario expected by farm producers has just come true. In other words, the position of the government opposite is completely at odds with what farm producers wanted.
It does not seem to worry our ministers opposite. However, I can tell you it does worry farmers in my riding, the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, Canadian Dairy Farmers and, I am sure, all Canadians who want a prosperous agricultural industry in this country.

This morning a number of my colleagues and I had the pleasure of meeting with the egg producers of eastern Ontario. Egg producers of some 15 or 20 constituencies in eastern Ontario met first with Liberal members of Parliament this morning. After our meeting they also met with Conservative members of Parliament. I am sure that members in this House who were at the meeting this morning will no doubt be aware of their tremendous concerns as well in regard to the GATT negotiations. They are concerned with the issue that I raised just moments ago, the aggregate measure of support issue. They are also concerned with this whole business of tariffication.

Supply
The tariffication issue basically involved a proposal, heaven forbid, whereby some of our supply management devices would be replaced by a so-called tariff equivalent eventually to be phased out in the future.
The government got us into the Canada-U.S. free trade deal nearly two years ago now- it feels like 25 years, but it has only been less than two years- whereby tariffs are gradually eliminated over 10 years. Let us assume for a moment that this government is so wrongheaded as to proceed with that policy of tariffication and then those tariffs are gradually decreased and eliminated pursuant to the trade deal.
It has an alleged 10-year phaseout even under the trade deal now, but obviously there comes a point at which the tariff fails to protect. Say, for instance, that the tariff established is deemed to be a value of 20 per cent for the purposes of the argument and it is phased out over 10 years, and that the advantage we have over the United States producer is only 5 per cent. Needless to say, after two and a half years the tariff ceases to give any protection at all. At that point when the U.S. product becomes cheaper than the Canadian one, no matter what tariff we have it will not do any good because the U.S. product will already be cheaper.
That is the point which I think needs to be raised and that is what is wrong with this whole business of getting into tariffication as a method of eventually replacing some of the supply management devices we have right now.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's poultry producers, the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency, the Canadian Ihrkey Marketing Agency, the Chicken Marketing Agency and the Chicken Broiler Marketing Agency got together and spelled out six objectives for the GATT negotiations. Here is a brief summary.
The maintenance of GATT Article XI: 2(c), the strengthening and
clarification of its code of interpretation-
With respect to improving the code of interpretation of Article
XI: 2(c):
-a flexible process of notice to GATT)
-a clear definition of goods including those that are controlled in a refrigerated or frozen form-
-a regulation governing a minimum contents of 50 per cent in the case of imports [-] concerning an end to unregulated imports of processed goods-
Thriff support only in the case of non-tariff barriers now illegal or contrary to GATT provisions-
The rejection of a proposition aimed at including programs under Article XI: 2(c)-
The maintenance of a well-established GATT principle that imports must given access proportionally to the market share held during a representative period-
The elimination of government export subsidies on a fair basis, taking into account the significant variations in current levels of support in the countries involved.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the positions set forth by the poultry producers. I told you earlier about the positions of the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec and of the Canadian Federation of Dairy Producers. But as usual it seems that the government opposite is not listening to anyone. If you never listen to anyone, Mr. Speaker, sooner or later you find yourself in a tight spot. I have the impression that by the time the next elections roll around-if it is not too late for the Canadian agricultural industry and if we still have farmers left after the devastating policies we get from the other side-the farming community will decide once and for all to get rid of the Conservative government.

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed my colleague's comments very much. I just wondered if he would comment on the fact that the figures for the aggregate measure of support that were used in the calculations that were tabled by the Government of Canada last week really reflect world prices, including their cost of production, or are they fire sale prices?
I noticed that eggs had used a price from the New York market. I do not know if this was for the last 25 cases at the end of the day that nobody wanted, or if they were really market prices. The milk prices came from selected border points along the Canada-U.S. border. Do you think that really reflects the world prices?
I would also like to ask him if he feels it is proper to go with such a measure of support based on these calculations when there is such a difference in input costs? Does he feel that if our costs and climatic conditions were equal to theirs, where we could pasture cattle for eight to 12 months of the year as they do in some of the American states, would we not be in a better position to compete under the current conditions and proposals as
English]


tabled? What do you think is the long-term future for dairy and poultry in Canada?

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad my colleague raised that issue. I had actually forgotten to mention that part of it when identifying what those prices have been over the last few years and their actual reflection of world prices, or at least what we normally understand as being world prices.
We are looking at the area of eggs particularly. I will use that example because it was raised this morning at a meeting that we had on prices that were abnormally low for the last three years. We are starting off with that base which is artificially low in the case of egg prices.
We are also using prices that were in effect in a period of the post-U.S. farm bill, if I can call it that. I think the actual date of implementation of the U.S. farm bill of 1985 was January 1, 1986. The U.S. farm bill contributed some $70 billion U.S. in farm subsidies so that the U.S. could recapture what it thought was its so-called rightful share of the world market.
What happened, of course, is that grain prices and the prices of a number of commodities were artificially lowered by the subsidies brought in by the United States. It follows quite reasonably from that that if prices are lowered on feed grain and beef-which has happened as a result of the U.S. farm bill and the so-called whole herd buy-out program-then prices are deflated on many agricultural commodities, not just those two. In the case of feed, obviously that is a product that is fed to the other animals, and in the case of beef it is a competitor to other meat products. When you lower the price of one, you lower the price of the others at the same time.
What we have, in fact, is an artificially low price period. That period of time is then utilized to make this base. Obviously the base is going to be incorrect. It is going to be artificially low.
To make matters worse, we do not have a similar low cost period to compare with in Canada because we did not have many of these exaggerated subsidies that they had south of the border. So we are comparing apples with oranges. To make matters even worse, as my colleague has pointed out, the input costs, property taxes, fuel costs, minimum wages and social benefits are different in Canada than in some of the U.S. states. A
Supply
further dimension to that is we have the climatic differences to deal with.
We may be good producers. We may be smart people in Canada, but we cannot recreate the weather of Louisiana and Georgia no matter how smart we are.
